title: The Stableman's Daughter: Holywell, the Firm, and the Stitch That Kept Her Name
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brazier Passage, Holywell, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of December 1841, in Brazier Passage off Holywell Street, a second daughter is born to Robert Burden, stableman, and his wife Ann, born Maizey, who has worked as a domestic servant and laundress. They name her Elizabeth; the household calls her Bessie. The passage runs behind a street the university keeps for its horses. Her elder sister Jane is a year and a half old; Mary Ann and William are older still. The whole household lives on a groom's wages.
suggested_refs: Brazier Passage off Holywell Street, Oxford, the Burden family's quarter

stops.name: St Peter-in-the-East, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of April she is carried up Queen's Lane to St Peter-in-the-East, the parish church of the Holywell district, and baptized Elizabeth Burden. The church is Norman under its later work, with a crypt older than the colleges around it. The register entry is the first document in which she exists. What follows it over the next eighty-two years is of the same order: census returns, addresses, and one stitch named in a printed handbook.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of St Peter-in-the-East, Queen's Lane, Oxford, April 1842

stops.name: Holywell Street, the stables at number 65
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the employment is attested, the year is a placeholder inside the girls' childhood
stops.campa: Robert Burden is employed as a stableman and later as a groom at 65 Holywell Street, servicing the coach and hunting traffic of a university town that does not employ his daughters. The family is poor. The two girls grow up inside the working economy of a street the colleges use and do not live on. What Bessie learns of needlework in this house no source records. Her mother has worked as a laundress and a domestic servant, the only trade near a needle that any source names in the household. The skill enters the documents already formed, in 1861, when Bessie is nineteen.
sources: Margaret Fleming, 'Where Janey Used to Live', Journal of the William Morris Society 4.4 (Winter 1981)
suggested_refs: 65 Holywell Street, Oxford, where Robert Burden worked as stableman and groom

stops.name: The Oxford Union, the murals and the faces they need
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Dante Gabriel Rossetti brings a company of young painters to Oxford to fresco the new Union debating hall with Arthurian subjects. William Morris is among them, twenty-three, painting and failing to paint. They need faces for Guenevere and for Iseult. The atlas keeps this pin already for william_morris, and keeps guinevere as a traveler in her own right; the queens of the mural cycle are about to be given the face of a groom's daughter from a street half a mile east of where the scaffolding stands.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Union murals of 1857, Rossetti's Arthurian cycle

stops.name: Theatre Royal, George Street, the evening the painters look up
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1857; day defaulted. The venue is a reconstruction: the source names only a performance in Oxford, and Oxford's theatre from 1836 stood on the corner of George Street
stops.campa: In October the Burden sisters go to a performance by the visiting Drury Lane Theatre Company. Rossetti and Burne-Jones, in Oxford for the Union murals, are in the same audience. They notice Jane and ask her to sit for them. No source says Bessie was noticed, and none says she was not. She is fifteen. Jane sits for Rossetti within months and marries Morris within two years. Bessie is in the audience by attestation and in nothing else the evening produced; the record keeps only the one name.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Royal, formerly the Vic, on the corner of George Street, Oxford

stops.name: St Michael at the North Gate, Jane marries William Morris
stops.date_confidence: attested; the church's own page gives 25 April, the mainstream date is 26 April, and the two are left unreconciled
stops.campa: Jane Burden marries William Morris at St Michael at the North Gate, the Saxon tower on Cornmarket. Whether Bessie stood in the church is documented nowhere consulted, though the family had no other Oxford to be in; the atlas records her presence as tradition and not as fact. The marriage makes a stableman's second daughter sister-in-law to a man who will spend his life arguing that the work of the hand is not beneath the work of the mind, and who will employ her hands for thirty-five years without printing her name.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical pin and date)
suggested_refs: St Michael at the North Gate, Cornmarket Street, Oxford

segments.name: The Firm, and the Months at Red House

stops.name: 8 Red Lion Square, the founding of the Firm
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Company opens at 8 Red Lion Square, offering carving, stained glass, metalwork, furniture, and embroidery. The embroidery is done by women. Mackail, writing the Life in 1899 with the founders' papers in front of him, names two of them and no others. Bessie Burden is not a partner and holds no share. She is in the trade list from the first year, under the head of a firm whose commercial signature will be a single man's name.
stops.quote: Mrs. Morris and her sister, Miss Burden, with several women working under them, executed embroidery on cloth and silk.
stops.quote_source: J. W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris, vol. 1 (London: Longmans, Green, 1899), p.154
sources: J. W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris, vol. 1 (1899), p.154, full text at archive.org
william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical pin and date)
suggested_refs: The prospectus of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., April 1861, naming embroidery among its trades

stops.name: Red House, the Legend of Good Women
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: sources give no consistent production dates for the series, only c.1860s; placed here at the midpoint of the Red House years
stops.campa: Morris designs a set of twelve large embroidered figures after Chaucer's Legend of Good Women for the walls of Red House. Seven are finished. Jane embroiders most of them; Bessie works beside her and takes two entirely. The Aphrodite is hers, and stays with the house, where the National Trust holds it. The St Catherine is hers, and travels to Kelmscott Manor, where the Society of Antiquaries holds it. The sources give no consistent date for either panel, or for the series they belong to.
sources: Society of Antiquaries of London, Kelmscott Manor collection
suggested_refs: The seven completed Legend of Good Women embroideries, of which Aphrodite and St Catherine are wholly Burden's

stops.name: Holywell Street, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1865; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Robert Burden dies at Oxford. His widow and unmarried daughter have no income of their own; the stables do not pay a pension. Bessie is twenty-three, unmarried, and holds a trade that has no professional standing in England and no institution to teach it in; the Royal School of Art Needlework is seven years away. The death removes the last thing keeping her in Oxford, and within months she is in the household of the sister who married well. She will live in Morris houses for most of the next thirty-five years.
suggested_refs: The Oxford burial register for Robert Burden, 1865, not located in this research pass

stops.name: Red House, moving in at the end
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the year 1865 is attested, the month is not. Widely repeated accounts placing her at Red House from 1860 are contradicted by the source they themselves cite
stops.campa: Bessie moves into Red House, the Bexleyheath house Philip Webb built for Morris and Jane, and finds a household already packing. Morris's health and the daily journey to London have decided him against the country. She arrives, by the record, a few months before the family leaves. The Red House of legend, the medieval dream with painted ceilings and unfinished murals, is for her a few months at the very end of it, not the five years the repeated version of the story hands her.
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath, built by Philip Webb for Morris, occupied 1860 to autumn 1865

stops.name: Red House, the house given up
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1865; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In the autumn the household gives up Red House and moves to London. Morris never sees the building again. Where each of the embroidered figures goes from here the sources do not follow; the Aphrodite Bessie stitched is at Bexleyheath still, in a house neither sister occupied for more than five years. She travels to London with them. She has no other household to go to, and the firm's embroidery has no more practised hand than hers; she is twenty-three and has been working for the Firm four years.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Red House embroidered hangings, autumn 1865

segments.name: Queen Square, the House That Is Also the Shop

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the workshops move to Bloomsbury
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1865; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The firm moves its workshops and the Morris family together into 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury, an eighteenth-century house with the business on the ground floor and the household above it. For Bessie this abolishes the distinction between the home she is kept in and the shop she works for. The embroidery room and the dining room are in the same building, and she is answerable in both. The arrangement holds thirteen years, and her first recorded address of her own does not appear until 1873.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical Queen Square pin)
suggested_refs: 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury, workshops and household of the Firm from 1865

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the block for Cupid Going Away
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the project's abandonment; the year she cut the block is not recorded
stops.campa: Morris plans an illustrated Earthly Paradise, hundreds of woodcuts after Burne-Jones, and needs cutters. Bessie is taught to cut and cuts the block for Cupid Going Away, one of the Cupid and Psyche series. The trial pages come out wrong, the type will not sit with the images, and the project is abandoned in 1868 to wait twenty-three years for the Kelmscott Press to solve it. Her block survives the abandonment. The design on it is Burne-Jones's; the cutting is hers.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, Earthly Paradise stop at Queen Square)
suggested_refs: The Cupid and Psyche woodblocks for the abandoned illustrated Earthly Paradise

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, entered as an embroiderer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1871 only; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The record of 1871 finds Elizabeth Burden at 26 Queen Square, London, entered as an embroiderer. The entry gives a name, an address, and an occupation, in a hand that is not hers. It does not give her as a sister or as a dependent of the household she is living in. She is twenty-nine and has been embroidering for the Firm ten years. In the same house the designs leaving the door are credited to William Morris, for commercial reasons the firm never concealed.
suggested_refs: The 1871 census return for 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the panel without the visit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tenancy; Burden's own presence at the house is undocumented at any date
stops.campa: Morris and Rossetti take the joint tenancy of Kelmscott Manor in Oxfordshire, Morris calling it heaven on earth and then leaving Jane there with Rossetti while he sails for Iceland. No document consulted places Bessie in the house on any date, and the atlas states that absence rather than filling it. What is at Kelmscott is her work: the St Catherine she embroidered entire is in the Society of Antiquaries' collection there, a Burden object at an address where her presence cannot be proved.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical pin and date)
Society of Antiquaries of London, Kelmscott Manor collection
suggested_refs: The St Catherine panel, Society of Antiquaries collection, Kelmscott Manor

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the letter to Aglaia Coronio
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1872; day defaulted
stops.campa: Morris writes to Aglaia Coronio from Queen Square in November, in the worst year of his marriage, with Rossetti at Kelmscott and Jane away. The letter's subject is not Bessie. She is what is in the room when the real subject cannot be written down. He calls her harmless and even good, blames himself for the irritation, and then names the exact nature of her position in the house in eight words. She is his wife's sister and his firm's embroiderer, and she is at his table every day.
stops.quote: I have been a good deal in the house here - not alone, that would have been pretty well - but alone with poor Bessy [sic]: I must say it is a shame, she is quite harmless and even good, and one ought not to be irritated by her - but O my God what I have suffered from finding always there at meals & the like! poor soul 'tis only because she is an accidental person with whom I have nothing whatever to do...
stops.quote_source: William Morris to Aglaia Coronio, November 1872, in Norman Kelvin (ed.), The Collected Letters of William Morris, vol. I, 1848-1880 (Princeton UP, 1984), p.172, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Burden'; the Kelvin page itself was not reachable in this pass
sources: Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Burden', block-quoting Kelvin vol. I p.172
Norman Kelvin (ed.), The Collected Letters of William Morris, vol. I (Princeton UP, 1984), p.172, not independently verified: archive.org lending-restricted, HathiTrust 403
suggested_refs: Kelvin's Collected Letters of William Morris, vol. I, the Coronio correspondence of 1872

stops.name: 100 Southampton Row, an address of her own
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1873; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: An address for her appears at 100 Southampton Row, a few minutes north of Queen Square. It is the first record of Bessie Burden living anywhere that is not a Morris household since her father died. She is thirty-one. In the same months she takes work at a school of needlework in Chelsea. The school pays women for the trade she has been doing under another name since 1861, and the address is her own. The letter calling her an accidental person is a year old.
suggested_refs: 100 Southampton Row, near Russell Square, London

stops.name: Sloane Street, the School of Art Needlework
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1873; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The School of Art Needlework has been on Sloane Street since 1872, an institution built to revive ornamental needlework as a serious art and to give paid work to women who need it. Bessie Burden arrives from the Queen Square workshops with more practical experience of large figure embroidery than the building holds, and no rank at all. She stays a few months. Whether she comes as a teacher or to advance her own technique the record does not settle; both readings appear in the sources and neither is documented.
sources: Royal School of Needlework, institutional history (Sloane Street from 1872)
suggested_refs: The Royal School of Art Needlework at its Sloane Street premises, 1872 onward

stops.name: Sloane Street, the quarrel over whose work it is
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; placed at the close of the first tenure in 1873 and marked as a placement, not a date
stops.campa: She leaves after a disagreement with the headmistress, Mrs Welby, over whose name goes on the students' work. The question is the one her working life turns on: the Firm credits its embroidery designs to William Morris, and the School credits its pupils' pieces to the School. Bessie Burden, anonymous inside one such arrangement since 1861, refuses the same arrangement when a second institution proposes it to her. No account of what was said survives.
sources: Lynn Hulse, 'Elizabeth Burden and the Royal School of Needlework', Journal of William Morris Studies 21.1, pp.22-34
suggested_refs: The Royal School of Art Needlework's early governance under Mrs Welby

stops.name: The School, the return in April
stops.date_confidence: attested April 1875 to 1877; day defaulted. The School's premises for these years are NOT established: its own history records Sloane Street from 1872 and Exhibition Road only from 1903, so the pin rests on Sloane Street for want of any documented alternative
stops.campa: She comes back to the School in April 1875 and teaches there two years. Where the School is housed in this interval is not established, and the pin sits on Sloane Street for want of a documented alternative. What she teaches is a laid and couched stitch of the kind seen in old Italian work, worked in graded rows so that a face or a limb can be rendered in flat silk without shading. It is a ground stitch used for flesh, which is not what it was designed for, and it works.
sources: Handbook of Embroidery (Royal School of Needlework, 1880), pp.49-50
Lynn Hulse, Journal of William Morris Studies 21.1
suggested_refs: The Royal School of Art Needlework's teaching staff lists, April 1875 to 1877

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Centennial and the flesh of Crane's figures
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Handbook attests the exhibited work but does not date it; the date given is the opening of the Centennial Exhibition
stops.campa: The School sends work across the Atlantic to the Centennial Exhibition at Philadelphia: large figures designed by Walter Crane for wall decoration, their flesh worked under Miss Burden's direction in the cushion stitch she brought into the building. Her name is not on the panels. It appears four years later, in print, in the School's own handbook, as the authority for the method. Bessie Burden is not in Philadelphia, and the stitch is worked there by the women she taught it to.
stops.quote: A variety of cushion stitch, which we frequently see in old Italian embroideries, was taught in the Royal School of Art-Needlework by Miss Burden, and used under her direction in working flesh in some large figures designed by Mr. Walter Crane for wall decoration, and exhibited at the Centennial Exhibition at Philadelphia.
stops.quote_source: Handbook of Embroidery (London: Royal School of Needlework, 1880), p.49
sources: Handbook of Embroidery (Royal School of Needlework, 1880), p.49, full text at Project Gutenberg ebook #24964
suggested_refs: Walter Crane's figure panels for the Royal School of Art Needlework, Centennial Exhibition, Philadelphia, 1876

stops.name: The School, the second tenure ends
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1877; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her second period at the School ends in 1877. She is thirty-five. Nothing consulted says whether she resigned, was dismissed, or simply reached the end of an engagement, and the quarrel of 1873 does not automatically explain 1877. After this date she holds no institutional post in London and returns to the work she has done since she was nineteen: embroidering, and supervising women who embroider, for a firm that will put another name on the result.
sources: Lynn Hulse, Journal of William Morris Studies 21.1
suggested_refs: Royal School of Art Needlework staff records for 1877, not located in this research pass

stops.name: The Handbook of Embroidery, the stitch is named in print
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication, 1880; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The School publishes its Handbook of Embroidery. On page fifty, describing a laid ground stitch, the compiler explains why the illustration is there at all. The stitch is named for a living woman who left the building three years earlier, and it is named because students keep asking what it is called. Burden stitch is the term. Nothing else she made is catalogued under her name until 1888. The Royal School of Needlework's stitch bank holds the entry today, under the same name.
stops.quote: It is really more suitable in its original character of a ground stitch than for working flesh. We have given an illustration of it, because we are so frequently asked to describe "Burden stitch."
stops.quote_source: Handbook of Embroidery (London: Royal School of Needlework, 1880), p.50
sources: Handbook of Embroidery (Royal School of Needlework, 1880), p.50, full text at Project Gutenberg ebook #24964
Royal School of Needlework Stitch Bank
suggested_refs: The 1880 Handbook of Embroidery, earliest printed use of the term Burden stitch

stops.name: Merton Abbey Works, the trade moves to the Wandle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Firm's relocation in June 1881; nothing places Burden herself on the site
stops.campa: Morris moves the dyeworks, looms and printing tables out of Bloomsbury to the old Merton Abbey works on the Wandle, water meadow with a river clean enough to rinse indigo. Embroidery is one of the trades that goes. No document consulted puts Bessie Burden on this ground, and the atlas records the pin on the strength of the trade rather than the woman. What is attested is that she was still working for the Firm through the eighties, and that the Firm was here.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical pin and date)
suggested_refs: The Merton Abbey Works on the River Wandle, Morris & Co. production site from 1881

stops.name: Castle Howard, three heroines out of Chaucer and Tennyson
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1880s only; year, month and day are defaults inside that decade
stops.campa: For Castle Howard in Yorkshire the two sisters embroider three panels of illustrious women out of Chaucer and Tennyson, figures of the kind Bessie has been making since Red House, now at the scale of a great house's wall. The panels are still there. It is one of the few of her works with a documented destination and a documented subject, and one of the few places where a source outside the Firm names both sisters together. Nothing dates them more closely.
suggested_refs: The three Morris embroidered panels of literary heroines at Castle Howard, Yorkshire

stops.name: The New Gallery, Regent Street, her own name in the catalogue
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1888; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society holds its first exhibition, founded on the principle that the maker of a thing should be named beside its designer. Elizabeth Burden sends three embroidered figures in silk and worsted: Helen of Troy, Hippolite, and Penelope. They are catalogued under her own name. She is forty-six. It is the first time in twenty-seven years of professional work that a public record of an object she made carries her name rather than William Morris's.
sources: Arts & Crafts Exhibition Society, catalogue of the first exhibition, 1888
suggested_refs: The 1888 catalogue of the first Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society show

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, the sister's house on the river
stops.date_confidence: attested for the house and the date as the atlas already holds them; Burden's own presence there is undocumented
stops.campa: Morris has held Kelmscott House on the Upper Mall since 1878, with the Socialist League meeting in the coach house and a carpet loom in the attic. The atlas pins this address at this date already for edward_bellamy, whose Looking Backward Morris read here and answered with News from Nowhere. No document consulted places Bessie Burden inside the house. Her sister lives here and her work is sold under the Firm's name from this address; the atlas marks her presence as an inference and not as a record.
sources: edward_bellamy.journey.json (atlas interlock, pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json)
suggested_refs: Kelmscott House, Upper Mall, Hammersmith, Morris's London home 1878 to 1896

stops.name: The Kelmscott Press, the old problem finished by other hands
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding of the Press; Burden has no documented connection to it
stops.campa: Morris founds the Kelmscott Press a few doors from the house and solves at last, with Emery Walker, the problem that killed the illustrated Earthly Paradise twenty-three years earlier: type and woodcut sitting on one page. Bessie Burden cut one of the blocks for that failed book. Nothing consulted connects her to the Press. The atlas keeps the pin because the problem she once worked at is being finished here, in a workshop she is not recorded as entering.
sources: william_morris.journey.json (atlas interlock, canonical pin and date)
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott Press at Hammersmith, founded January 1891

segments.name: Surrey, and the End of the Record

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Morris dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Morris dies at Kelmscott House at sixty-two. Bessie Burden is fifty-four. She has worked for his firm, under his name, since 1861, and has lived in his households for most of the years between. Whatever the letter of 1872 meant by an accidental person, the accident lasted the length of his adult life. The Firm continues without him, and so does she for a while, and then the London part of her life closes without any document recording why. No obituary consulted names her at all.
suggested_refs: Morris's funeral at Kelmscott, October 1896

stops.name: Redhill, Surrey, out of London
stops.date_confidence: the sources say only after 1901; this is an earliest bound and not an attested year, and month and day are defaults
stops.campa: Some time after 1901 she leaves London for Redhill in Surrey, a railway town on the Brighton line half an hour from the city and entirely outside it. She is sixty. No source consulted gives a reason, a street, or a month. What the sources give is the fact of the move and the fact that she does not stop working: in Redhill she teaches needlework, which is what she has done in one room or another since she was thirty-one, and now does for schoolgirls.
suggested_refs: Redhill, Surrey, on the London to Brighton line

stops.name: Boldrewood, Redhill, the needlework class
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: attested only as after 1901, with no year given; 1905 is a placeholder inside that bound and the school's street address was not located
stops.campa: She teaches needlework at Boldrewood, a school for young ladies in Redhill. The street address was not located in this pass, so the pin sits on the town. The stitch named after her is by now in the English embroidery handbooks, and the girls learning it from her here have no reason to know that the Royal School printed her name in 1880 only because its students kept asking what the stitch was called. She is teaching, in a market town, the thing she was not credited for in London.
suggested_refs: Boldrewood school for young ladies, Redhill, Surrey, exact address not located

stops.name: Reigate, Surrey, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the town is contradicted by one summary consulted, which names Redhill instead, and the two are left unreconciled
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August 1924 Elizabeth Burden dies at Reigate in Surrey, aged eighty-two. She has outlived William Morris by twenty-eight years and the founding of the Firm by sixty-three. The England and Wales death index carries the registration. A second summary consulted names Redhill, the adjoining town, instead of Reigate; the two are a mile and a half apart, and the atlas records both rather than quietly averaging them. Nothing in the register distinguishes her from any other elderly woman of the town.
sources: England & Wales Civil Registration Death Index, 1916-2007
WikiTree summary consulted 2026-08, which names Redhill
suggested_refs: The England and Wales death registration for Elizabeth Burden, third quarter 1924

stops.name: Reigate, the grave that is not located
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no burial date and no burial place are documented anywhere reachable; the date is three days after death, a convention only
stops.campa: Where she is buried is not documented in anything reachable. The reference works file her among burials in Surrey without naming a churchyard, a cemetery, or a plot, and the standard grave database returned a refusal to the machine that asked. So the last stop of the life is a gap, and is stated as one. The surname is on a stitch still taught in English needlework schools; the grave is unlocated, and finding it would take a parish or cemetery register in Reigate or Redhill read on the ground.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Burden' (category tag only, no burial text in the body)
Findagrave, HTTP 403, inaccessible in this pass
suggested_refs: Reigate and Redhill parish and cemetery burial registers, 1924, unconsulted

stops.name: Holywell, Where Janey Used to Live
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Winter 1981 issue, volume 4 number 4, pages 2 to 17; day defaulted
stops.campa: Margaret Fleming publishes Where Janey Used to Live in the Journal of the William Morris Society, walking the Holywell streets to reconstruct what the Burden family's circumstances actually were, against a century of Pre-Raphaelite mythology about Jane's origins. Bessie appears in it as part of the household. The article runs sixteen pages, and it is the closest thing that exists to a study of what the Burden family's Oxford circumstances actually were.
sources: Margaret Fleming, 'Where Janey Used to Live', Journal of the William Morris Society 4.4 (Winter 1981), pp.2-17
Fiona MacCarthy, William Morris: A Life for Our Time (Faber and Faber, 1994)
suggested_refs: Fleming's 1981 walk about Holywell, and the Society of Antiquaries' later Jane's People, Passages and Places

stops.name: Sloane Street, the one article about her
stops.date_confidence: the article is attested as volume 21 number 1, pages 22 to 34, per the William Morris Society's own index; the commonly quoted year 2014 and season Winter are NOT confirmed by that listing and are given here as unverified
stops.campa: Lynn Hulse publishes Elizabeth Burden and the Royal School of Needlework in the Journal of William Morris Studies, the first study to treat Burden's teaching as a career rather than as an episode in her sister's life. The volume and issue are confirmed by the Society's own index; the year usually cited with it is not, and is carried here as unverified. So far as this research pass could establish, it is the only dedicated scholarly article on her, ninety years after her death.
sources: Lynn Hulse, 'Elizabeth Burden and the Royal School of Needlework', Journal of William Morris Studies 21.1, pp.22-34, per the William Morris Society index
suggested_refs: Journal of William Morris Studies vol. 21 no. 1, the Hulse article on Burden at the RSN

stops.name: The William Morris Gallery, Walthamstow, her name on a label
stops.date_confidence: no date: this stop marks a present-day holding located during the 2026 research pass, not a dated event. The specific object reported could NOT be confirmed and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The William Morris Gallery at Walthamstow holds embroidery under her name; a collection record is cited for it. A specific piece, an Angel Minstrel with Cymbals of about 1885 labelled with her dates, is reported, but the gallery's own search returned only its interface to this pass and the object could not be confirmed. Elsewhere in the atlas leo_chiachio and daniel_giannone embroider a whole household into a gallery under both their names. The atlas notes the rhyme and claims no thread between them.
